title: The Bacterium in the Insulin Bottle

pages.text: Every morning, Grace’s grandfather, Papa Jacob, injected a small dose of insulin. He had diabetes, which means that his body could not manage sugar in his blood without help. Insulin works like a key: it tells the body’s cells to take sugar out of the blood and use it. One day, Grace picked up the little bottle. “Papa,” she asked, “where does insulin come from?” Papa Jacob smiled. “From a laboratory,” he said. “But ask your science teacher about the bacteria.” Grace blinked. “Bacteria?”

pages.alt: A girl holds a small insulin bottle while her grandfather prepares an injection at a table.

pages.text: Mr Enchill drew a bacterium on the board, with a tiny loop of DNA inside. “Long ago,” he said, “insulin for people with diabetes came from the pancreas of pigs and cows. It took an enormous amount of animal tissue. In 1923, about ten thousand pounds of pancreas were needed to make one pound of pure insulin. Supply was limited, and for some people the animal insulin caused reactions.”

“Long ago,” he said, “insulin for people with diabetes came from the pancreas of pigs and cows.
It took an enormous amount of animal tissue.
In 1923, about ten thousand pounds of pancreas were needed to make one pound of pure insulin.
Supply was limited, and for some people the animal insulin caused reactions.”
pages.alt: A teacher draws a bacterium and a pig and cow on a board with arrows to a bottle.

pages.text: “Then scientists had an idea,” he continued. “In 1973, researchers showed they could cut open a loop of bacterial DNA, put in a gene from another living thing and close it again. A few years later, a team in the United States made the human insulin gene work inside bacteria. The bacteria multiplied in large tanks and produced insulin identical to the human kind. In 1982, the first such medicine was approved.” Grace’s mouth fell open. “Bacteria,” she said, “make my grandfather’s insulin.”

In 1982, the first such medicine was approved.” Grace’s mouth fell open.
“Bacteria,” she said, “make my grandfather’s insulin.”
pages.alt: A teacher shows a diagram of a DNA loop with a gene inserted and bacteria in a tank.

pages.text: “And the story gets better,” said Mr Enchill. “In 1964, a scientist visited hot springs in Yellowstone Park in the United States and found bacteria living in water that would cook most living things. Years later, scientists isolated an enzyme from one of those bacteria that does not break down in heat. That enzyme became the heart of a method called PCR, which works like a molecular photocopier: using cycles of heating and cooling, it makes millions of copies of one chosen piece of DNA that already exists. PCR is used in disease testing and in forensic science, which identifies people from tiny samples.” Grace’s eyes shone. “From a hot spring,” she whispered.

“From a hot spring,” she whispered.
pages.alt: A teacher points to a picture of a steaming hot spring with a tiny microbe drawn beside it.

pages.text: “One more,” said Mr Enchill. “A Chinese scientist, Tu Youyou, searched an ancient medical text about a plant called sweet wormwood. Her team isolated artemisinin from it, and in 2015 she shared the Nobel Prize for the discovery. The Nobel committee said that artemisinin-based treatments save more than a hundred thousand lives a year in Africa. As a separate example of a lucky discovery, in 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould had landed on a dish of bacteria and killed those near it. That mould led to penicillin.” He paused. “Every one of these came from living things that few people noticed.”

pages.text: “Does Ghana have any?” asked Grace. “We have wonderful plants,” said Mr Enchill. “For example, the root of a plant called nibima, Cryptolepis sanguinolenta, has long been used by Ghanaian herbalists. Researchers at the Centre for Plant Medicine Research report promising laboratory results. But I must be honest: laboratory results are not proof of a medicine, and no one should replace proper malaria treatment with a plant. It shows only how much is still to be studied.”

pages.text: A boy asked, “So should we protect every species because it might give us medicine?” Mr Enchill thought. “That is one reason, and the strongest form of it is the precaution argument. We cannot tell in advance which species will matter, and once a species is gone, it is gone for ever. But I will be honest again: most species will not become medicines. We also protect them because forests and rivers depend on them, because they are part of our heritage, and because we have a duty not to destroy what we do not understand.”

pages.text: For homework, the class wrote how human insulin is made. Grace wrote: “First, scientists identify the gene that carries the instructions for human insulin. Next, they insert the gene into a loop of bacterial DNA. Then the bacteria are grown in large tanks, where they multiply and produce insulin. After that, the insulin is separated and purified. Finally, it is tested and put into bottles for patients.”

pages.alt: A girl writes the steps of insulin production at a desk with a bottle beside her.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: when you explain a process, use sequence words such as “first”, “next”, “then”, “after that” and “finally”, write in the present tense, and use full words. Grace’s paragraph can be followed step by step. She did not claim more than she knew, and she checked each fact. A good scientist is a careful, honest writer. The end.
